name: Offline password cracking (§3)
description: Feed recovered hash material — kerberoast and AS-REP tickets, NTLM/NTDS dumps, captured NetNTLMv2, /etc/shadow entries — to hashcat or john and recover the plaintext. It all runs offline on your own box and touches no target, so these steps auto-advance; a cracked hash stays a candidate secret until a real login proves it.

actions.title: Identify an unknown hash
actions.hypothesis: Pinning down the hash format before cracking keeps you from burning hours on the wrong hashcat mode.
actions.proves: the likely hash type and cracker mode to use (hashcat --identify records hash.type{mode})
actions.does_not_prove: anything about the plaintext behind it

actions.title: Crack a kerberoast (TGS) hash
actions.hypothesis: Service accounts frequently use weak, human-chosen passwords, so a cracked $krb5tgs$ ticket hands you the service account's plaintext.
actions.proves: the plaintext password recovered from a kerberoast hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack an AS-REP roast hash
actions.hypothesis: An account without Kerberos pre-auth is AS-REP-roastable: the $krb5asrep$ hash it yields cracks to that user's plaintext.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from an AS-REP hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a dumped NTLM hash
actions.hypothesis: An NTLM hash pulled from SAM or NTDS may crack to a plaintext that logs in here or is reused elsewhere.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from an NTLM hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a login on its own — and note the NT hash is already usable for pass-the-hash without any cracking

actions.title: Crack a captured NetNTLMv2 hash
actions.hypothesis: A NetNTLMv2 hash captured by Responder or a relay cracks to the account's plaintext; unlike an NT hash it cannot be passed, so cracking is the only route.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a NetNTLMv2 capture
actions.does_not_prove: a working login until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a Linux /etc/shadow hash
actions.hypothesis: A shadow entry you can read (via a SUID binary, a backup, or a misconfig) cracks to a local password that is often reused for sudo.
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a shadow hash (a candidate credential)
actions.does_not_prove: a login or sudo right until that credential is actually used

actions.title: Crack a Password-Protected Archive (zip/rar/7z)
actions.hypothesis: A password-protected backup/export archive found in loot usually hides config files or credentials. Extract its hash with the matching *2john and crack it offline; then unpack it on your box and paste anything credential-like from inside back on Evidence.
actions.proves: the archive password (a candidate secret until it unlocks the archive and its contents are read back)
actions.does_not_prove: any access — the password only unlocks the file; what's inside must still be extracted and validated

commands.note: for a .zip — use the archive obol flagged as loot.material
john auto-detects the *2john format; unzip with the cracked password, then paste any creds/config from inside on Evidence.

actions.title: Online password brute over SSH (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: When SSH is reachable and no working credential is known yet, a targeted hydra run against an enumerated user list can recover a login — a noisy, lockout-risky attack, so it is approve-tier and never auto-fires in a normal cruise.
actions.proves: a working SSH login (hydra's success line parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra actually returns a hit

commands.note: seed users.txt from the enumerated user list; -t 4 keeps SSH stable; -f stops on first hit. Mind lockout policy (policy.lockout).

actions.title: Online password brute over FTP (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: A reachable FTP service with no known credential is a classic hydra target; a recovered login often reuses onto other services.
actions.proves: a working FTP login (parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra returns a hit

commands.note: seed users.txt from enumeration; watch the lockout policy.

actions.title: Online password brute over RDP (hydra)
actions.hypothesis: A reachable RDP service with no known credential can be sprayed with hydra; go slow to avoid account lockout.
actions.proves: a working RDP login (parses to a validated credential)
actions.does_not_prove: anything until hydra returns a hit

commands.note: -t 1 (single thread) is important for RDP; lockout risk is high — prefer a small, targeted list.

actions.title: Crack an MS Cache v2 (DCC2) hash
actions.hypothesis: Domain Cached Credentials v2 ($DCC2$) are stored on a workstation so a domain user can log in offline. They are deliberately slow to crack, but a weak password still falls — and the plaintext is a real domain credential to reuse. Pulled from a local secretsdump (the cachedump).
actions.proves: the plaintext recovered from a cached domain credential (DCC2)
actions.does_not_prove: a fast result — DCC2 is intentionally slow; and the hash cannot be passed (unlike NTLM), so cracking is the only use
